prompt.context: Your client is a small Berkeley-based café chain called CoffeeCo. CoffeeCo has four café locations in and around the UC Berkeley campus. CoffeeCo has been experiencing declining profit margins over the past several years. The owner of the store wants to know why this is happening and what they can do about it. The chain has invested a lot in store expansions, opening one new store in each of the past two years.
prompt.question: Why are CoffeeCo's profit margins declining and what can they do about it?

clarifying_info.a: Since the locations are on or around campus, the customers are 80% students and 20% faculty/staff.

clarifying_info.q: Has the customer population changed over the past several years?
clarifying_info.a: The population has been roughly flat.

clarifying_info.q: Has spend per customer or café usage changed?
clarifying_info.a: The store owner says spend per customer has been flat.
The café market near UC Berkeley has always been competitive but has not become more so over the past several years.

clarifying_info.q: Have there been any new substitutes for coffee or cafés?
clarifying_info.a: No major replacements for coffee/cafés have emerged in the Berkeley market.
CoffeeCo sells two products: Coffee and Sandwiches.
Two original stores are adjacent to campus (both on Bancroft) and two new stores are on campus (one at Haas, one at the Law School).

clarifying_info.q: How have the old stores been performing?
clarifying_info.a: Old store financial performance has stayed the same since 2010.

exhibits.title: Selected CoffeeCo Income Statement Items
exhibits.shows: Three-year income statement with Revenue, COGS, and OpEx figures for 2010, 2011, and 2012 (values in thousands). Footnote states all store openings occurred on Jan 1 of their corresponding fiscal year and opened fully operational.

exhibits.title: Menu for Old Stores vs. New Stores
exhibits.shows: Side-by-side menu comparison for old stores (adjacent to campus) and new stores (on campus), showing which products each store type offers and their approximate share of revenue.

framework: Start with market analysis: assess whether external factors (demand, competition, substitutes) explain the margin decline
Move to internal financials: analyze revenue, COGS, and OpEx trends in total, then on a per-store basis
Disaggregate new stores vs. old stores to isolate the underperforming unit(s)
Diagnose the revenue gap at new stores: product mix / menu differences
Diagnose the OpEx gap at new stores: labor cost drivers (hours and wage structure)
Synthesize findings into a recommendation with risks and next steps

questions.prompt: Has the market changed in a way that could explain CoffeeCo's declining profitability?
questions.guidance: A strong candidate presents a structured market analysis framework (demand side: customers, population, spend per customer; supply side: competition, substitutes) before diving in. The answer is that the market has NOT materially changed — population is flat, spend per customer is flat, competition is unchanged, no new substitutes. Market forces are NOT driving the decline. A better candidate knows when they have enough information to move on without prompting.

questions.prompt: Looking at Exhibit 1, what is driving the decline in profit margins? Analyze on a total and per-store basis, and compare new vs. old stores.
questions.guidance: Candidate should compute margins and per-store averages. Key observations: (1) Gross margin is unchanged at 50% — COGS is NOT the issue. (2) OpEx margin is rising (20% in 2010, 25% in 2011, 28% in 2012) — OpEx IS a problem. (3) On a per-store basis, revenue per store has declined and OpEx per store has risen. (4) Isolating new vs. old stores shows old stores stayed at 2010 levels; new stores are generating ~$100K less revenue and ~$50K more OpEx per store than old stores. The candidate should conclude that new stores are the root cause.

math.setup: Compute per-store averages for 2010 and 2012, then estimate new store vs. old store performance in 2012 assuming old stores held 2010 levels.
steps: Old stores in 2012 (assume same as 2010): 2 stores x $500K = $1,000K revenue
New stores in 2012 (residual): $1,800K - $1,000K = $800K revenue for 2 new stores = $400K per new store
Revenue gap: $500K (old) - $400K (new) = $100K less per new store
Old store OpEx 2012 (assume same as 2010): 2 stores x $100K = $200K
New store OpEx 2012 (residual): $500K - $200K = $300K for 2 new stores = $150K per new store
OpEx gap: $150K (new) - $100K (old) = $50K more per new store
Old store operating profit margin: $150K GP - $100K OpEx = $50K? No — old store GP = $250K, OpEx = $100K, profit = $150K (30% margin)
New store operating profit: $200K GP - $150K OpEx = $50K (12.5% margin vs. 30% for old stores)
math.answer: New stores generate $100K less revenue and incur $50K more OpEx per store than old stores, compressing operating margin from 30% to 12.5% per new store.

questions.prompt: Why are the new stores generating less revenue than the old stores?
questions.guidance: When candidate gets to the revenue issue, hand them Exhibit 2 (Menu for Old Stores vs. New Stores). The new stores do not offer sandwiches, which represent ~20% of revenue at old stores. This explains the ~$100K revenue gap per store. The underlying reason is that the new on-campus stores cannot make sandwiches due to kitchen permitting issues on campus.

math.setup: Estimate the revenue impact of not offering sandwiches at new stores.
steps: Sandwiches ~20% of old store revenue: $500K x 20% = $100K per store
New stores have no sandwich revenue, so they forgo ~$100K per store
math.answer: Not offering sandwiches costs new stores approximately $100K in revenue each, matching the observed revenue gap.

questions.prompt: Why are the new stores incurring higher OpEx than the old stores? Brainstorm the drivers of labor expense.
questions.guidance: When candidate gets to the OpEx issue, hand them the OpEx breakout exhibit (Exhibit 3 / exhibit_p068). The entire $50K OpEx increase at new stores is due to higher labor expense ($90K labor at new stores vs. $40K at old stores). Candidate should decompose labor expense as: Labor = hours worked x effective hourly wage per hour. Key info to provide when asked: (1) New stores have longer operating hours than old stores but experience little traffic during extra periods. (2) Base hourly wage is the same at both stores, but new stores have substantial overtime charges while old stores do not. Solution: CoffeeCo should reduce hours at new stores and/or add more employees to reduce overtime pay.

math.setup: Labor expense comparison between old and new stores.
steps: Old store labor expense: ~$40K per store
New store labor expense: ~$90K per store
Labor gap: $90K - $40K = $50K per new store — accounts for the entire OpEx increase
Labor = hours worked x effective hourly wage; new stores have more hours AND higher effective wage due to overtime
math.answer: New stores pay ~$50K more in labor per store due to longer (low-traffic) hours and overtime charges, fully explaining the OpEx gap.

brainstorming.prompt: What are the drivers of labor expense at the new stores, and what can CoffeeCo do to fix the OpEx issue?

categories.name: Hours Worked
ideas: New stores are open longer hours with little incremental traffic during extra periods
Reducing store hours during low-traffic periods would lower total hours worked
Aligning open hours to peak demand (campus schedule) could cut wasted labor hours

categories.name: Effective Hourly Wage
ideas: Base hourly wage is the same at old and new stores
New stores incur substantial overtime charges, raising the effective hourly rate
Adding more part-time employees to cover shifts would reduce overtime exposure
Restructuring shift schedules to stay within standard hours eliminates overtime premium

categories.name: Revenue-Side Fix for New Stores
ideas: Start selling sandwiches made off-campus and brought to on-campus stores to get around kitchen permitting issues
Introduce a limited grab-and-go food menu that does not require on-site food prep
Explore whether permitting issues can be resolved to enable on-site sandwich preparation

recommendation: CoffeeCo's profit margin decline is caused by its two new on-campus stores, which generate $100K less revenue and incur $50K more OpEx per store than the original locations
The revenue shortfall stems from an inability to sell sandwiches at new stores due to kitchen permitting issues on campus
The OpEx overrun is driven by unnecessarily long operating hours and overtime labor charges at the new stores
CoffeeCo should begin making sandwiches off-site and transporting them to the new stores to recover lost sandwich revenue
CoffeeCo should reduce operating hours at new stores to match actual demand patterns and add staff to eliminate overtime
risks: Sandwiches made off-site may suffer quality or freshness issues, potentially damaging the brand
Labor optimization (hour reductions) could harm employee morale or service levels
Permitting and logistics for off-site sandwich production add operational complexity
next_steps: Assess logistics and economics of off-site sandwich production and delivery to new stores
Analyze hourly traffic data at new stores to identify optimal reduced operating hours
Model the financial impact of eliminating overtime through additional part-time hires vs. reducing hours
Explore whether kitchen permitting on campus is feasible to enable in-store sandwich preparation longer-term
